title: Nerves and hormones: the body's fast messages and slow messages

summary.text: Your body does some things before you decide, and sends some messages through the blood. How fast are they? In this unit you will test what your body does before you choose, time a hormone message with water, and see what makes your mouth water with a lemon.
summary.art: A child of nine pulling her hand back from a hot steel pot, with a thin yellow line drawn from her fingertip up her arm to her backbone and back to her arm muscle.

intro.hook: You step on a sharp plastic brick in the dark. Your foot lifts before you can say 'ow'. You did not choose to lift it. So who told your leg to move?
intro.text: A nerve carried the message. It went from your foot to your spinal cord, which runs inside your backbone. The spinal cord sent a message straight back to your leg muscles. Your brain heard about it a moment later. A quick answer like this is called a reflex. Your body also sends slow messages. They are chemicals called hormones, and they travel in your blood. A hormone told your bones to grow this year. In this unit you time a slow message with two tumblers of water. You also test a reflex with drops of lemon juice.
intro.art: A bare foot lifting off a small plastic toy brick on a dark floor, with a child's surprised face above.

outcomes: I can say what a nerve signal is, and how it passes from one nerve cell to the next.
I can say what a hormone is, and how it reaches the parts of the body.
I can compare nerve messages and hormone messages: how fast, how far and how long.
I can explain what a reflex is, and trace a reflex through the spinal cord.
I can explain why a hormone reaches every cell but changes only some of them.
I can time a message in my own body with a fair test, and say what my results show.
I can give examples of nerves and hormones working together.
I can tell how scientists found out that some messages travel in the blood.

terms.meaning: A cell that carries messages. Most neurons have one long thin fibre, like a thread.
terms.example: One neuron runs from your lower back to your big toe. It is about as long as your leg.
terms.art: A single nerve cell with a round cell body, short branches at one end and one very long thin fibre.

terms.meaning: A bundle of many nerve fibres wrapped together, like the wires inside a cable.
terms.example: A nerve runs behind your elbow. When you bump it, your little finger tingles.
terms.art: A cut-open cable showing many thin threads inside, next to a drawing of an arm with a line running down it.

terms.meaning: A tiny electrical change that travels along a nerve fibre from one end to the other.
terms.example: When a mosquito lands on your arm, a nerve signal travels from the skin to your spinal cord.
terms.art: A long nerve fibre with a small bright pulse drawn partway along it and an arrow showing its direction.

terms.meaning: An atom that carries a small electric charge. Sodium and potassium ions carry nerve signals.
terms.example: Table salt in water breaks up into sodium ions and chloride ions.
terms.art: A pinch of salt falling into a tumbler of water, with tiny dots marked plus and minus spreading out.

terms.meaning: The tiny gap where a neuron passes a message on to the next cell. Chemicals carry the message across.
terms.example: A message from your fingertip crosses at least two synapses before it reaches your brain.
terms.art: The swollen end of one nerve fibre almost touching another cell, with small dots crossing the narrow gap between them.

terms.meaning: A thick rope of neurons inside your backbone. It links your brain to the rest of your body.
terms.example: Run a finger down the bumps of your backbone. The spinal cord is inside those bones.
terms.art: A side view of a child's back with the backbone drawn as a row of small bones and a pale cord running through them.

terms.meaning: A quick answer that your body gives without waiting for you to decide.
terms.example: You blink when something flies at your eye. Your mouth waters when sour juice touches your tongue.
terms.art: A child blinking as a small paper ball flies towards her face.

terms.meaning: The path that a reflex message takes. It runs from a sensor to the spinal cord or brain stem, and out to a muscle or gland.
terms.example: Your fingertip touches a hot pot. A signal runs up an arm nerve to the spinal cord. Then it runs back down an arm nerve to an arm muscle. That whole path is one reflex arc.
terms.art: A simple line drawing of an arm and backbone with arrows going from a fingertip to the backbone and back to the upper arm.

terms.meaning: A chemical message that a gland puts into the blood. The blood carries it to the whole body.
terms.example: Growth hormone tells your bones to grow longer.
terms.art: A blood vessel drawn as a red tube with small coloured dots flowing along inside it.

terms.meaning: A group of cells that makes something and sends it out. Some glands make hormones, and some make sweat, tears or saliva.
terms.example: The pancreas is a gland behind your stomach. It makes the hormone insulin.
terms.art: An outline of a child's body with small coloured shapes at the base of the brain, in the neck, behind the stomach and above the kidneys.

terms.meaning: A tiny part on or in a cell that one kind of hormone fits, as a key fits a lock.
terms.example: A heart muscle cell has receptors for adrenaline. A hair has no receptors, because the part of a hair that you can see is not alive.
terms.art: A round cell with small cup-shaped parts on the surface, and one small shape fitting exactly into one cup.

terms.meaning: A cell that has the receptor for a hormone. Only target cells answer that hormone.
terms.example: The cells of the kidney tubes are target cells for the hormone ADH.
terms.art: Many cells in a row with the same small dots drifting past all of them, and only two cells lit up.

terms.meaning: A hormone from two small glands above the kidneys. It gets the body ready for sudden hard work.
terms.example: After a sudden fright, adrenaline keeps your heart beating hard for some minutes.
terms.art: A child with a hand on her chest after a dog has barked behind her, with two small glands marked above the kidneys in an inset.

terms.meaning: A hormone that tells the kidneys to save water. It is released by a small gland under the brain.
terms.example: On a hot day you have more ADH in your blood. So you make less urine, and the urine is darker.
terms.art: Two kidneys with a small gland drawn under the brain above them, and a dotted arrow running from the gland down to the kidneys.

explanations.concept: The body has two ways to send a message
explanations.definition: A nerve message is a signal that travels along nerve fibres to one place. A hormone message is a chemical that travels in the blood to the whole body.
explanations.description: Your body is made of trillions of cells, and they must work together. To do that, they send messages. Nerves are the fast way. A nerve message travels along a fibre, and it arrives in a fraction of a second. It goes only where that fibre goes, so it can reach one muscle and no other. Hormones are the slow way. A gland puts a chemical into the blood. The heart pumps the blood round the whole body in about one minute. So a hormone reaches every part, and its effect can last for minutes, hours or years. The body uses nerves for jobs that must be quick and exact. It uses hormones for jobs that are slow, long or spread over the whole body.
examples: Nerve: you feel a tap on your shoulder and turn your head at once.
Nerve: your fingers move over the keys of a harmonium.
Hormone: your bones grow a few centimetres longer each year.
Hormone: after a meal, sugar moves out of your blood and into your muscles.
explanations.art: A child's body outline drawn twice: one with thin yellow lines branching from the backbone, the other with red blood vessels and small coloured dots flowing through them.

explanations.concept: A nerve signal is a wave of electrical change moving along a fibre
explanations.definition: A nerve signal is a short electrical change that moves along a nerve fibre. It is made by ions crossing the skin of the fibre.
explanations.description: A nerve fibre is a long, thin part of a neuron. Salty liquid lies inside it and outside it. The salt is there as ions, which are atoms with a small electric charge. When a signal starts, tiny gates open in the skin of the fibre. Sodium ions rush in at that spot. This makes the gates just ahead open too, and so the change moves along. The ions themselves hardly travel. The change is what travels, as a fall travels along a row of dominoes. The fastest nerve fibres carry a signal at about 100 metres per second. The slowest carry it at about 1 metre per second. Electricity in a copper wire is millions of times faster. After each signal, tiny pumps push the ions back, and this uses energy from food.
examples: A row of dominoes falls from one end to the other, but each domino stays in place.
Fast fibres tell you where your foot touched the floor.
Slow fibres carry a dull ache, which is why an ache arrives after the first sharp pain.
explanations.art: A long nerve fibre in close-up with small gates along its skin, tiny dots rushing in through the open gates at one spot, and an arrow showing the change moving along.

explanations.concept: At a synapse, a chemical carries the message across a gap
explanations.definition: A synapse is the tiny gap between a neuron and the next cell. A chemical crosses the gap and starts a signal on the other side.
explanations.description: Neurons do not join up like soldered wires. At the end of each fibre there is a gap, thousands of times thinner than a hair. An electrical signal does not jump that gap. Instead, the end of the fibre lets out a tiny puff of a chemical. The chemical drifts across in about one thousandth of a second. On the far side it fits into receptors and starts a new signal. So every nerve message is partly electrical and partly chemical. Each synapse adds a small delay. A path with few synapses is faster than a path with many. A synapse is also a place where a message can be made stronger, made weaker or stopped.
examples: Where a nerve fibre meets a muscle, the chemical tells the muscle to shorten.
A dentist's injection stops signals in a nerve, so the tooth's message never reaches the brain.
Learning a skill changes how strongly some synapses pass messages on.
explanations.art: A close-up of the end of one nerve fibre and the surface of the next cell, with small dots crossing the narrow gap and fitting into cup-shaped receptors.

explanations.concept: A reflex takes the short path
explanations.definition: A reflex is a quick answer that the body gives without waiting for a decision. Its message takes a short path called a reflex arc.
explanations.description: Suppose your fingers touch a hot pot. Sensors in the skin start a signal. It travels up a nerve in your arm to your spinal cord. Inside the spinal cord it crosses one or two synapses. Then a signal goes straight back down another fibre to the muscle that bends your elbow. Your hand pulls away in a fraction of a second. At the same time, the spinal cord sends the news up to your brain. That path has more synapses, so the feeling of pain comes a moment after your hand has moved. Some reflexes pass through the brain stem, the lowest part of the brain. Blinking, sneezing and mouth-watering are like this. Your brain can change some reflexes a little. You can hold a hot cup of tea for a second longer if you must.
examples: Your foot lifts off a sharp stone before you feel the pain.
You blink when a paper ball flies at your face.
Your mouth waters when sour lemon juice touches your tongue.
A doctor taps below your kneecap and your leg kicks.
explanations.art: A child's arm and backbone drawn in outline, with one arrow from the fingertip to the spinal cord, a second arrow back to the upper arm muscle, and a dotted arrow going up to the brain.

explanations.concept: A hormone is a chemical message in the blood
explanations.definition: A hormone is a chemical that a gland puts into the blood. It changes what certain cells do, often far away from the gland.
explanations.description: Glands that make hormones have no tubes. They put their hormones straight into the blood that flows through them. The blood carries each hormone to every part of the body. A hormone works in very small amounts. The adrenaline in your blood is about as dilute as one drop in a large swimming pool. A hormone message is slow to start, because the gland must release it and the blood must carry it. It is also slow to stop. The hormone stays in the blood until the liver and kidneys break it down or remove it. Adrenaline is cleared in a few minutes. Other hormones last for hours. The gland can keep on releasing a hormone for years, as it does with growth hormone.
examples: Insulin from the pancreas tells cells to take sugar in from the blood.
ADH from a gland under the brain tells the kidneys to save water.
Growth hormone from the same gland tells bones to grow longer.
Thyroid hormone from a gland in the neck sets how fast cells use energy.
explanations.art: A small gland with blood vessels running through it, tiny dots leaving the gland into the blood, and the same dots shown far away near a kidney.

explanations.concept: Only cells with the right receptor answer a hormone
explanations.definition: A receptor is a part of a cell that one kind of hormone fits. A cell answers a hormone only if the cell has the receptor for that hormone.
explanations.description: A hormone in the blood passes almost every cell in the body. Most cells take no notice. A cell answers only if they have a receptor that the hormone fits, as a key fits a lock. Cells with the receptor are called target cells. Kidney tube cells have receptors for ADH, so ADH changes what the kidneys do. One hormone can also give different orders to different cells. Adrenaline fits receptors on heart cells, liver cells and the muscle cells round your airways. The heart beats harder. The liver lets sugar out into the blood. The airways widen. Each kind of cell does their own job when the same key turns their lock.
examples: A radio programme goes out everywhere, but only a radio tuned to that station plays it.
Some asthma inhalers hold a medicine that fits the adrenaline receptors of the airways.
A person whose cells lack a working receptor does not respond to that hormone, however much is in the blood.
explanations.art: Three different cells labelled heart, liver and airway, each with the same small key-shaped dot fitting a lock on its surface, and a small picture of what each cell then does.

explanations.concept: Fast and brief, or slow and lasting
explanations.definition: Nerve messages are fast, go to one place and stop quickly. Hormone messages are slower, go everywhere and last longer.
explanations.description: Compare the two kinds of message in three ways. The first is speed. A nerve message arrives in a fraction of a second. A hormone takes from seconds to hours to show its effect. The second is where the message goes. A nerve fibre ends at one place, so its message is exact. A hormone goes wherever blood goes. The third is how long the message lasts. A nerve message ends when the signals stop. A hormone goes on working until the body has cleared it from the blood. Each way suits different jobs. Catching a ball needs speed and one exact muscle. Growing needs a steady message to many kinds of cells for years. No body could do both jobs well with only one kind of message.
examples: Pulling a hand off a hot tawa: nerves.
Growing 6 centimetres in a year: hormones.
Keeping the right amount of water in the blood all day: hormones.
Writing your name: nerves.
explanations.art: A two-column chart with a running postal worker carrying one letter to one door on the left, and a slow river carrying many small boats past many doors on the right.

explanations.definition: Many things the body does use both kinds of message. Often a nerve message starts the answer and a hormone keeps it going.
explanations.description: A dog barks suddenly behind you. Nerves act first. You jump and turn within a fraction of a second. Other nerves run to the two adrenal glands above your kidneys. Within seconds these glands put adrenaline into your blood. Your heart beats hard and your liver lets out sugar. The dog walks away, but the adrenaline is still in your blood. Your heart goes on pounding for some minutes. The brain also links the two systems directly. A small part of the brain called the hypothalamus checks the blood. Just below it hangs the pituitary gland, the size of a pea. The hypothalamus tells the pituitary which hormones to release. So the nervous system and the hormone system are two parts of one message system.
examples: A sudden fright: nerves make you jump, and adrenaline keeps your heart pounding.
Evening: your eyes tell your brain that the light is fading. A gland in the brain then releases the sleep hormone melatonin.
A drink of water: sensors in the brain notice the change in the blood. The pituitary gland then releases less ADH.
explanations.art: A child jumping as a dog barks behind her, with a yellow line from ear to brain to legs marked 'first', and red dots spreading from glands above the kidneys marked 'second'.

explanations.description: Plants have no neurons. Yet plants sense, decide and send messages through their bodies. They use hormones. A hormone called auxin gathers on the shady side of a shoot, and the shoot bends towards the light. A ripe banana gives off a gas hormone that tells nearby fruit to ripen. Plants also send electrical signals. Touch a touch-me-not, and an electrical signal travels along the leaf at about 2 centimetres per second. The leaflets fold as it passes. In 2018 scientists filmed a signal spreading from a bitten leaf to other leaves within a few minutes. Scientists agree on these findings. They disagree about what to call them.
examples: A touch-me-not folds their leaflets one pair after another, as the signal passes along.
A money plant in a dim room bends their shoots towards the window.
A raw mango ripens sooner in a bag with a ripe banana.

perspectives.who: Plant scientists such as Jagadish Chandra Bose, and later Stefano Mancuso and Frantisek Baluska
perspectives.explanation: Plants carry electrical signals and use some of the same chemicals that animal neurons use. Bose measured such signals in Kolkata more than a hundred years ago. These scientists say plants have their own kind of signalling system, and they study it under the name plant neurobiology.

perspectives.who: Plant scientists such as Amedeo Alpi and more than 30 others, writing in 2007
perspectives.explanation: Plants have no neurons and no synapses, so the word 'neurobiology' misleads. On this view the signals are real, but they are automatic responses. They are better described in the plant's own terms.

explanations.art: A touch-me-not plant with one leaf half folded, a finger just lifted away, and small arrows showing the folding moving along the leaf.

explanations.concept: Where the message systems came from
explanations.description: Chemical messages are far older than nerves. Bacteria give off chemicals that other bacteria sense and act on. They were doing this billions of years before any animal lived. Sponges are animals with no neurons at all. Their cells still signal to each other with chemicals, and a sponge can squeeze their whole body slowly. Jellyfish have a net of neurons spread through the body, with no brain. Animals with a head and a tail came later, and their neurons gathered into a brain and a cord. Scientists think the first neurons appeared more than 600 million years ago. Nobody knows exactly how. One idea is that neurons began as ordinary cells that sent chemical messages to their neighbours. Over time some of them grew long fibres. The chemical was then let out at the far end of the fibre, right next to its target. If so, a synapse works like a hormone message that has been made very small and very private. The chemical goes only to the one cell next to it.
examples: Bacteria in a group sense how many neighbours they have by the chemicals around them.
A sponge has no nerves, yet they can slowly squeeze water out of their body.
An octopus has about two thirds of their neurons in their arms.
explanations.art: Four small pictures in a row: a cluster of bacteria with dots between them, a sponge, a jellyfish with a net of lines inside the bell, and a fish with a brain and a cord.

agreed.text: A nerve signal takes time to travel, and it is far slower than electricity in a wire.
agreed.evidence: In 1850 Hermann von Helmholtz timed a signal along a frog's nerve. It travelled at about 27 metres per second.

agreed.text: A nerve signal is made by ions crossing the skin of the nerve fibre.
agreed.evidence: In 1952 Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley measured the ions crossing the giant nerve fibre of a squid. This fibre is up to 1 millimetre thick, so a fine wire can be put inside it.

agreed.text: Reflexes can run through the spinal cord without the brain.
agreed.evidence: Charles Sherrington studied reflexes for many years and described their paths in a book in 1906. People whose spinal cord is cut off from the brain by an injury still have a knee kick.

agreed.text: Some messages travel in the blood and not along nerves.
agreed.evidence: In 1902 William Bayliss and Ernest Starling cut every nerve to a piece of gut. Acid in that piece still made the pancreas pour out juice.

agreed.text: Hormones work in very small amounts, and those amounts can be measured.
agreed.evidence: In 1959 Rosalyn Yalow and Solomon Berson found a way to measure insulin in a small sample of blood. Yalow, a physicist, won a Nobel Prize for it in 1977.

agreed.text: A hormone acts only on cells that have a receptor for it.
agreed.evidence: In the 1970s Robert Lefkowitz's team tagged a hormone with a radioactive label. They found the receptors it stuck to on cells, and later worked out what the receptor is made of.

challenging.claim: A nerve signal is electricity flowing along a nerve, just as it flows along a copper wire.
challenging.who: Many people, since Luigi Galvani made a frog's leg twitch with electricity in the 1780s.
challenging.for: A nerve signal is an electrical change, and instruments can pick it up through the skin.
challenging.against: Helmholtz measured about 27 metres per second in a frog's nerve. Electricity in a wire is millions of times faster. In a wire, tiny particles called electrons flow along it. In a nerve, ions cross the skin of the fibre at one spot after another.

challenging.claim: The brain controls everything the body does.
challenging.who: A common belief, and many older school books.
challenging.for: The brain does take part in almost everything, and it can change many body actions.
challenging.against: A reflex runs through the spinal cord and starts before the brain hears of it. The gut has its own net of neurons and moves food along without orders from the brain. Glands such as the pancreas sense the blood and answer directly.

challenging.claim: All the body's messages travel along nerves.
challenging.who: Ivan Pavlov and most scientists before 1902.
challenging.for: Pavlov had shown that nerves control saliva and stomach juice.
challenging.against: Bayliss and Starling cut the nerves to a piece of gut. Its message still reached the pancreas through the blood.

challenging.claim: Nerves and hormones are really one message system.
challenging.who: Berta Scharrer and Ernst Scharrer, from 1928 onwards.
challenging.for: The Scharrers found neurons that release hormones into the blood, in fish, insects and mammals. The brain's hypothalamus is made of such cells. Adrenaline is a hormone, and a close relative of it carries messages across synapses.
challenging.against: For years most scientists did not accept that a neuron could act as a gland. The two kinds of message still differ in speed and in where they go, so the two names stay useful.

challenging.claim: Plants have something like a nervous system.
challenging.who: Scientists who named a new field 'plant neurobiology' in 2006.
challenging.for: Plants carry electrical signals from leaf to leaf. They sense, remember and decide.
challenging.against: Plants have no neurons and no synapses. Many plant scientists accept the signals but reject the name.

challenging.claim: In an emergency, adrenaline can give a person the strength to lift a car.
challenging.for: Adrenaline sends more blood and sugar to the muscles. A person in danger may also ignore pain and use muscles harder than they usually dare.
challenging.against: Nobody has measured such strength in a test, because it would be wrong to frighten people that badly. The stories cannot be checked.

big_questions.q: Your hand pulls back from a hot pot before you feel pain. Who decided to move it?
big_questions.hint: The message turned round in your spinal cord. Is your spinal cord part of 'you'?

big_questions.q: A hormone passes every cell, but only cells with the receptor answer. Is the hormone still a message to the cells that do not answer?
big_questions.hint: Think of a letter written in a language you cannot read. Is it a message for you?

big_questions.q: After a fright your heart pounds for minutes. Is the fear in your brain, in your blood, or in both?
big_questions.hint: In 1884 the thinker William James asked whether we feel afraid because our heart pounds.

big_questions.q: Your kidneys, your heart and your gut each answer messages without asking your brain. Where in your body are you?
big_questions.hint: There may be more than one good answer.

big_questions.q: Hormones were found by tests on dogs. In one test, the dog was put to sleep with a drug and did not wake up again. The finding has helped millions of people. Was the test right?
big_questions.hint: People argued about this in London at the time. Laws on such tests are much stricter now.

big_questions.q: A plant has no nerves, yet a bitten leaf sends a signal to the other leaves. What does a body need in order to send a message?
big_questions.hint: Think about a sender, a path and a receiver that can answer.

story.title: The Last Line of the Kolam
story.note: Yazhini, Malar Chithi and their Pongal morning are made up. These facts are real. A hand pulls back from a hot thing by a reflex through the spinal cord. The feeling of pain comes a moment later. A fright makes the adrenal glands above the kidneys put adrenaline into the blood. Adrenaline makes the heart beat hard and the hands tremble, and the body clears it in some minutes. Cool running water is the right first aid for a small burn.
text: On the morning of Pongal, Yazhini had one job. It was the last line of the kolam.

Her aunt, Malar Chithi, had drawn the rest before sunrise. White lines of rice flour looped round a grid of dots, across the whole courtyard of the house in Madurai. In the middle stood three bricks, a wood fire and a new clay pot of milk and rice. Only the border was left.
"The border is yours," Chithi had said. "One line, all the way round, without lifting your hand."
Yazhini had practised that line on the back step for a week. Now she took a pinch of flour between her thumb and two fingers. She let it run out in a thin white thread, the way Chithi did.

She was halfway along the first side when the pot hissed. A tongue of milk foam was climbing over the rim. It was too early. Nobody was ready to shout. Yazhini did not stop to think. She put out her left hand to steady the pot.

Her hand came back before she knew it had gone. She was already sitting on the ground, holding her fingers against her chest, when the pain arrived. It came like a late guest, a whole moment after the hand had left the pot.

"Show me." Chithi was beside her. She was a nurse at the big hospital, and she looked at burns every week. Two fingertips were pink. She led Yazhini to the tap by the back door and held the fingers under the running water. "Not ice. Just water. We stay here until I say."

The water was cool, and the pain grew small. But something else was wrong. Yazhini's heart was banging. Her knees felt loose. She held out her good right hand, the kolam hand. It trembled like a leaf on the neem tree.
"I am not scared," she said. "It is over. Why am I shaking?"
"Because two messengers went out," said Chithi, "and only one has come home."

She turned Yazhini's wet hand over. "The first one ran along your nerves. Finger to backbone, backbone to arm. Pull! It did not wait to ask your head. It was there and back before the pain reached you. That messenger has finished."
"And the second?"

"The second is not a runner. It is a pinch of something poured into your blood, from two small glands that sit above your kidneys. It is called adrenaline. Your blood has carried it to every part of you. It told your heart to beat hard. It told your liver to put sugar into your blood. It made your muscles ready to run from a fire." She smiled. "Nobody has told it yet that the fire is only a Pongal pot."
"Then tell it to stop."

"Nobody can call it back. A nerve message stops when the nerve stops. What is in the blood stays there until your body has broken it down. That takes some minutes." She put the fingers back under the tap. "Keep them here. By the time they are cool, your hand will be yours again."
From the courtyard came her grandfather's voice. "The milk is rising! Where is the border?"

Yazhini pulled her hand out of the water. "I can do it now." She ran back, took a pinch of flour, and began. The line came out like the track of a beetle. It shook left and right, thick and thin. After one hand's length she stopped and stared at it.
Chithi did not scold. She walked Yazhini back to the tap and put the burnt fingers under the water again.

So Yazhini waited. It was the hardest part of the morning. The foam was climbing in the pot. Her cousins were gathering with steel plates and spoons to bang. She counted her breaths, slow in and slower out, the way Chithi showed her.
Somewhere between sixty and seventy she noticed that her heart had gone quiet. She had not felt it stop banging. It had only, at some point, stopped.
She held out her right hand. It lay on the air as still as a plate on a shelf.
"Now," said Chithi.

Yazhini knelt at the place where the shaky line ended. She did not rub it out. She took her pinch of flour and went on from there. The white thread ran out smooth and even, round the first corner, along the long side, round the second. She joined the end to the beginning just as the milk rose over the rim and ran down the side of the pot.
"Pongalo Pongal!" shouted the cousins, and the spoons crashed on the plates.
Yazhini jumped at the noise. Then she laughed, and felt her heart begin to knock again.
"There it goes," she said. "The second messenger."
"Give it a few minutes," said Chithi, and went to stir the pot.
That evening the border was still there. One hand's length of it shook like a beetle's track, and all the rest ran straight. Yazhini's grandfather wanted to know who had spoiled the corner.
"Nobody spoiled it," said Yazhini. "That part was drawn while the message was still in my blood."
story.epiphany: Yazhini's hand pulled back from the pot at once, because a nerve message is fast and ends quickly. Her hand went on shaking for minutes, because adrenaline stays in the blood until the body breaks it down. She could draw a steady line only after the slow message had faded.
ask: Why did Yazhini's hand move before she felt the pain?
Why could nobody make the shaking stop at once?
When has your heart gone on pounding after a fright was over?
