printables.title: 20 message cards: something the body does on the front, the messenger and the reason on the back

items.f: Your hand jerks back from a hot tawa.
items.b: Nerve. Within seconds. This is a reflex through the spinal cord.

items.f: A child grows 6 centimetres taller in one year.
items.b: Hormone. Minutes or longer. Growth hormone tells the bones to grow, month after month.

items.f: You blink when a ball flies at your face.
items.b: Nerve. Within seconds. Blinking is a reflex through the brain stem.

items.f: After a big meal, sugar moves out of your blood and into your muscles.
items.b: Hormone. Minutes or longer. The pancreas releases insulin, and cells take the sugar in.

items.f: You feel a mosquito land on your arm.
items.b: Nerve. Within seconds. Sensors in the skin send a signal to the brain.

items.f: You drink a lot of water. An hour later your pee is pale.
items.b: Hormone. Minutes or longer. Less of the hormone ADH is released, so the kidneys let more water out.

items.f: You hear your name and turn your head.
items.b: Nerve. Within seconds. The message goes from ear to brain to neck muscles.

items.f: A dog barks behind you. You jump, and your heart pounds for minutes.
items.b: Both. The nerve part is within seconds. The hormone part takes minutes or longer. Nerves make you jump. Adrenaline in the blood keeps the heart pounding.

items.f: The evening grows dark, and by bedtime you feel sleepy.
items.b: Both. The nerve part is within seconds. The hormone part takes minutes or longer. Nerves from the eyes report the dark. Then a gland in the brain releases melatonin.

items.f: Your mouth waters when you bite a sour raw mango.
items.b: Nerve. Within seconds. Nerves from the tongue reach the brain stem, and nerves tell the saliva glands to work.

items.f: A tadpole turns into a frog.
items.b: Hormone. Minutes or longer. Thyroid hormone tells the tadpole's body to change, over some weeks.

items.f: You kick a football.
items.b: Nerve. Within seconds. The brain sends signals down the spinal cord to the leg muscles.

items.f: A girl of twelve grows quickly and her body changes shape.
items.b: Hormone. Minutes or longer. Hormones start these changes, and the changes take years.

items.f: Food leaves your stomach, and your pancreas pours out juice to digest it.
items.b: Hormone. Minutes or longer. The gut wall releases the hormone secretin into the blood. Nerves help too, so 'Both' also scores.

items.f: You sneeze when dust tickles the inside of your nose.
items.b: Nerve. Within seconds. Sneezing is a reflex through the brain stem.

items.f: A mother hears her baby cry, and her milk begins to flow.
items.b: Both. The nerve part is within seconds. The hormone part takes minutes or longer. Nerves carry the sound to her brain. A hormone in her blood tells the breast to let the milk out.

items.f: You lift your foot off a sharp stone.
items.b: Nerve. Within seconds. This is a reflex through the spinal cord.

items.f: Your pupils get smaller when you walk into bright sunlight.
items.b: Nerve. Within seconds. This is a reflex. Nerves tell a ring of muscle in the eye to tighten.

items.f: You skip lunch, and your liver puts stored sugar back into your blood.
items.b: Hormone. Minutes or longer. The pancreas releases the hormone glucagon, which tells the liver to do this.

items.f: You shiver on a cold morning in Ooty.
items.b: Nerve. Within seconds. The brain senses the cold and sends nerve signals that make the muscles shake.

printables.title: 3 messenger tokens: Nerve, Hormone, Both. Print one set for each player

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every other player puts one token face down: Nerve, Hormone or Both. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches the back scores 1 point.
A player can score 1 more point. Before the back is read, they say 'within seconds' or 'minutes or longer'. If the back agrees, they get the point.
With two players, swap the reader's role after every card. The reader does not guess on their own card.
Playing alone? Read a card, say the messenger and the time aloud, then turn the card over. Score yourself.
After all 20 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, try to beat your score next time.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile. Give each player one set of three tokens.
flow.say: Each card describes something a body does. A message made it happen. Your tokens say who carried the message: nerves, hormones or both.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take three tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Nerve, Hormone or Both. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first ten cards. After each card, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after card five.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Choose a token and put it face down. Now turn it over. The reader reads the back. Who scored?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: How did you decide between nerve and hormone?
good: I asked how fast it happens.
A quick answer in one place is a nerve.
A slow change in the whole body is a hormone.

flow.parent: A useful question for a stuck child: does this happen in a second, or does it take minutes? One child can play alone or with you.
flow.context: In this step of Nerve, Hormone or Both you play the first ten message cards.

flow.do: Play the last ten cards the same way. Keep the score on a piece of paper.
flow.say: Ten more cards. This time, also say 'within seconds' or 'minutes or longer' before the back is read. A right answer earns one more point.
flow.kid: Play ten more cards. Say how long each message takes.
flow.context: In this step of Nerve, Hormone or Both you play the last ten cards and also guess the time.

flow.do: Count the points. Then sort all 20 cards into three piles: Nerve, Hormone and Both. Look at the piles together.
flow.say: Let us sort the cards into three piles. What is the same about all the cards in the nerve pile? What is the same in the hormone pile?
flow.kid: Sort the cards into three piles. What is the same in each pile?

check.q: Which job suits a hormone better than a nerve?
options: Telling bones to grow for years
Pulling a hand off a hot pot
Turning the head towards a sound
check.why: Growing is slow, lasts for years and involves many kinds of cells. A hormone in the blood reaches them all. Pulling a hand away and turning the head must happen at once, in one place, so nerves do them.

flow.context: This is the last step of Nerve, Hormone or Both. You sort the message cards into piles and compare the piles.

games.title: Who Has the Lock? The receptor game
games.context: This is a card game about receptors. A hormone reaches every cell in the body. You work out which cells have the lock that the hormone fits.

setup.art: Twelve small cards dealt out in front of two players, each card showing the name of a kind of cell, and a pile of four larger cards between them.
setup.caption: 1. Deal the 12 cell cards, fronts up. Put the 4 hormone cards in a pile.

setup.art: A child reading the top hormone card aloud while another player pushes three of her cell cards forward.
setup.caption: 2. Read a hormone card. Push forward each cell that you think has the lock.

setup.art: The pushed cards turned over to show the words on their backs, and a score being written on paper.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the pushed cards over. Score 1 for each right card. Lose 1 for each wrong card.

printables.title: 4 hormone cards: the hormone on the front, what each target cell does on the back

items.f: ADRENALINE is in the blood. The glands above the kidneys released it after a fright. Who has the lock?
items.b: Heart muscle cell: beats harder and faster. Liver cell: lets sugar out into the blood. Leg muscle cell: breaks down stored sugar for quick energy. Fat cell: lets fat out as fuel. Airway muscle cell: relaxes, so the airways widen. Skin blood vessel cell: tightens, so the skin turns pale. Pupil muscle cell: pulls the pupil wide.

items.f: INSULIN is in the blood. The pancreas released it after a meal. Who has the lock?
items.b: Liver cell: takes sugar in and stores it. Leg muscle cell: takes sugar in from the blood. Fat cell: takes sugar in and stores it as fat.

items.f: ADH is in the blood. A gland under the brain released it because the body is short of water. Who has the lock?
items.b: Kidney tube cell: lets more water go back into the blood. So there is less pee, and it is darker.

items.f: GROWTH HORMONE is in the blood. A gland under the brain released it during deep sleep. Who has the lock?
items.b: Bone growth cell: divides, so the bone grows longer. Liver cell: sends out a second growth signal to the rest of the body.

printables.title: 12 cell cards: a body part and its job on the front, the locks on the back

items.f: Heart muscle cell. Job: squeezes to pump blood.
items.b: Lock for: adrenaline.

items.f: Liver cell. Job: stores sugar and lets it out again.
items.b: Locks for: adrenaline, insulin and growth hormone.

items.f: Leg muscle cell. Job: shortens to move the leg.
items.b: Locks for: adrenaline and insulin.

items.f: Fat cell. Job: stores fuel as fat.
items.b: Locks for: adrenaline and insulin.

items.f: Airway muscle cell. Job: sets how wide the air tubes of the lungs are.
items.b: Lock for: adrenaline.

items.f: Skin blood vessel cell. Job: sets how much blood flows through the skin.
items.b: Lock for: adrenaline.

items.f: Pupil muscle cell. Job: pulls the pupil of the eye wider.
items.b: Lock for: adrenaline.

items.f: Kidney tube cell. Job: decides how much water leaves in the pee.
items.b: Lock for: ADH.

items.f: Bone growth cell, near the end of a long bone. Job: makes the bone longer.
items.b: Lock for: growth hormone.

items.f: Hair, the part above the skin. Job: covers and protects.
items.b: No locks. The hair above the skin is not made of living cells.

items.f: Fingernail tip. Job: protects the fingertip.
items.b: No locks. The nail tip is not made of living cells.

items.f: Tooth enamel, the hard outside of a tooth. Job: bites and grinds.
items.b: No locks. Enamel has no living cells in it.

rules: Shuffle the 12 cell cards and deal them all out, fronts up. Nobody looks at the backs. Put the 4 hormone cards in a pile, fronts up.
One player reads the front of the top hormone card aloud. That hormone is now in the blood, so it reaches every card on the table.
Every player pushes forward each of their cell cards that they think has a lock for that hormone.
Turn the pushed cards over. A card with that lock scores 1 point. A card without it loses 1 point. A card that was not pushed scores nothing.
Read the back of the hormone card aloud. It says what each target cell does. Then turn every cell card front up again.
Play all 4 hormone cards. Then each player passes their cell cards to the player on their left, and you play the 4 hormones again.
The player with the most points after both rounds wins. The cards show the main locks only. Real cells have many more.
Playing alone? Use all 12 cell cards. Each round has 13 right cards in all. Try to reach 13 in the second round.

flow.do: Cut out the 16 cards. Deal the 12 cell cards, fronts up. Put the 4 hormone cards in a pile. Read the rules together.
flow.say: A hormone travels in the blood, so it passes every cell. Only a cell with the right lock answers. A lock is called a receptor.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Deal the cell cards. Do not look at the backs.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Has the Lock. You set up the hormone cards and the cell cards.

flow.do: Play the first round with all 4 hormone cards. Read the back of each hormone card aloud after the scoring.
flow.say: The first hormone is in the blood. Which of your cells has a lock for it? Push those cards forward. Then we turn them over.
flow.kid: Listen to the hormone. Push forward the cells with its lock. Check the backs.
flow.parent: The first round is mostly guessing, and that is fine. The backs teach the answers. The second round shows what was learned.
flow.context: In this step of Who Has the Lock you play the first round and learn which cells have which locks.

flow.do: Swap cell cards with another player. Play the 4 hormone cards again and add up both rounds.
flow.say: Pass your cell cards to the left. Now you have cells you did not hold before. What do you remember about them?
flow.kid: Swap your cell cards. Play the four hormones again.
flow.context: In this step of Who Has the Lock you play the second round with new cell cards.

flow.do: Lay all 12 cell cards with the backs up. Count how many cards have a lock for adrenaline and how many for ADH. Talk about the question below.
flow.say: Count the cells with a lock for adrenaline. Now count the cells with a lock for ADH. Why might one hormone have so many targets?
flow.kid: Count the adrenaline locks. Count the ADH locks. Why are they so different?

ask.q: Why does adrenaline have locks on so many kinds of cell?
good: Running from danger needs the heart, the lungs, the muscles and the liver all at once.
The whole body has to get ready.
ADH has one job, in the kidneys.

check.q: A hormone reaches every cell in the blood's path. Why do only some cells answer?
options: Only some cells have its receptor
It only reaches cells near the gland
check.why: A receptor is the lock that the hormone fits. A cell without that receptor is passed by. If you chose 'cells near the gland', remember that blood carries the hormone everywhere in about a minute.

flow.context: This is the last step of Who Has the Lock. You count the locks for each hormone and ask why they differ.

experiments.title: The Water Message Test: how long does a hormone message take?
experiments.question: After you drink 2 tumblers of water, how many minutes pass before your kidneys send the extra water out? What happens on a day when you take only 4 sips?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After 2 tumblers of water, how many minutes will pass before you need the toilet? Will it be different after only 4 sips? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Do both days at the same time of day, at least one hour after a meal or a big drink. Start each day by emptying your bladder in the toilet. Use the same tumbler on both days. Sit and do quiet things during the wait on both days. Do not eat or drink anything else until the test ends. Only one thing changes: 4 sips of water on day 1, and 2 tumblers on day 2.
results_table: Minutes until I needed the toilet

materials.item: drinking water, 2 tumblers (about 400 millilitres in all)
a steel or glass tumbler that holds about 200 millilitres
a clock or a phone timer
a pencil and a notebook page for the results

schedule.what: Guess. Empty your bladder, take 4 sips of water, and check every 15 minutes for up to 90 minutes.
At the same time of day, empty your bladder, drink 2 tumblers of water, and check every 15 minutes. Then compare the two days.

experiments.record: Draw a table with two rows, one for each day. Write the drink, the minutes until you needed the toilet, the colour of the pee and your slow count. If you did not need the toilet in 90 minutes, write 'more than 90'.
experiments.context: In this two-day experiment you drink 4 sips of water on one day and 2 tumblers on the next. You time how long your kidneys take to send the extra water out.

setup.art: A child coming out of a bathroom door and looking at a wall clock, with a notebook and pencil on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Empty your bladder in the toilet. Write down the time.

setup.art: The same child drinking from a steel tumbler, with a second full tumbler beside her on the table.
setup.caption: 2. Day 1: take 4 sips. Day 2: drink 2 tumblers within 5 minutes.

setup.art: The child reading a book on a mat while a phone timer on the floor shows 15 minutes.
setup.caption: 3. Sit quietly. Every 15 minutes, rate how much you need the toilet, from 0 to 3.

setup.art: A notebook table with two rows marked Day 1 and Day 2 and columns for minutes, colour and count.
setup.caption: 4. When you go, write the minutes, the colour and your slow count.

flow.do: Show your child the tumbler. Explain the two days. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: On one day you will take 4 sips of water. On the next day you will drink 2 tumblers. How many minutes after the 2 tumblers will you need the toilet? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will drink 2 tumblers of water. When will you need the toilet? Why?

ask.q: What has to happen inside you between the drink and the toilet?
good: The water goes to my stomach.
It gets into my blood.
My kidneys take it out.
It fills my bladder.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children guess 5 minutes, because they picture the water running straight through. Choose a time when your child last ate or drank a lot more than an hour ago.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Water Message Test. You guess how long your body takes to send out 2 tumblers of water.

flow.do: Day 1. Your child empties their bladder in the toilet. They take 4 sips of water. Write down the time. Draw the results table.
flow.say: First go to the toilet, so that we start empty. Now take 4 sips of water and no more. I am writing down the time.
flow.kid: Go to the toilet first. Then take 4 sips of water. Write the time.
flow.context: In this step of the Water Message Test you start day 1. You empty your bladder and take 4 sips of water.

flow.do: Set a timer for every 15 minutes, for up to 90 minutes. Each time, your child rates how much they need the toilet, from 0 to 3. When they need to go, they go, and they count slowly while they pee. Write the minutes, the colour and the count.
flow.say: How much do you need the toilet now? Say 0 for not at all, 1 for a little, 2 for clearly and 3 for now. If it reaches 2 or 3, go, and count slowly while you pee.
flow.kid: Every 15 minutes, rate your need from 0 to 3. Count slowly while you pee.
flow.wait: Check every 15 minutes for up to 90 minutes
flow.parent: Your child can read, draw or do the term cards during the wait, but not run about. On most days there is little or no need within 90 minutes after 4 sips. Write 'more than 90' and stop. The slow count is a rough measure of how much pee there was.
flow.context: In this step of the Water Message Test you check every 15 minutes on day 1, after 4 sips.

flow.do: Day 2, at the same time of day. Your child empties their bladder. They drink 2 tumblers of water within 5 minutes. Write down the time when the second tumbler is finished.
flow.say: Go to the toilet first, as you did before. Now drink both tumblers of water. Take up to 5 minutes. I am writing down the time.
flow.kid: Go to the toilet first. Then drink 2 tumblers of water. Write the time.
flow.wait: Do this the next day, at the same time of day
flow.parent: Two tumblers is a safe amount. More water does not make a better test, so keep to two.
flow.context: In this step of the Water Message Test you start day 2. You empty your bladder and drink 2 tumblers of water.

flow.do: Check every 15 minutes as on day 1. When your child needs the toilet, write the minutes, the colour and the slow count. Go on checking until 90 minutes have passed, because there may be a second visit.
flow.say: How much do you need the toilet now, from 0 to 3? When you go, look at the colour and count slowly. Then come back, because we go on checking.
flow.kid: Rate your need every 15 minutes. When you go, check the colour and count.

check.q: In the Water Message Test, why do you empty your bladder before each drink?
options: So both days start the same
check.why: A fair test changes only one thing. If the bladder were half full on one day, you would need the toilet sooner for that reason alone. If you chose 'the kidneys stop working', remember that kidneys work all day and night.

flow.parent: On most days the need arrives 30 to 60 minutes after the drink. There is more pee than usual and it is pale. On a hot day, or after a lot of play, the body keeps more of the water. Then the wait is longer. Write down what really happens.
flow.context: In this step of the Water Message Test you check every 15 minutes on day 2, after 2 tumblers.

flow.do: Put the two rows of the table side by side. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at both days. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Your tongue felt the water at once. Why did your kidneys answer so much later?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Your tongue felt the water in less than a second. Why did the kidneys take so long?
good: The water had to get into the blood first.
The message to the kidneys is slow.
The message goes by blood, not by a nerve.

ask.q: Why was the pee paler on the day with 2 tumblers?
good: There was more water in it.
The kidneys let the extra water out.

flow.parent: The reason has several steps. The water passes from the gut into the blood, which takes roughly 10 to 20 minutes. Sensors in the brain notice that the blood is a little more watery. A gland under the brain then releases less of the hormone ADH. ADH tells the kidneys to save water. The ADH already in the blood fades slowly. About half of it is gone every 15 minutes. Only then do the kidneys let the extra water out. No nerve carries this order to the kidneys. The last step is a nerve message: the full bladder tells the brain.
flow.think: On a hot afternoon after a game, would the Water Message Test take a longer or a shorter time? Why?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Water Message Test. You compare the day with 4 sips and the day with 2 tumblers, and say what the results show.

experiments.title: The Lemon Test: what makes your mouth water?
experiments.question: Does your mouth make more saliva when lemon juice touches your tongue? Does it also happen when you only think about a lemon, or only smell one?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which will make your mouth water most: thinking about a lemon, smelling a lemon, or tasting lemon juice? Will thinking alone do anything? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Count swallows for exactly 2 minutes in every round. Keep your lips closed, and swallow only when your mouth feels full. The same person counts every time. Rest for 1 minute and take one sip of water between rounds. The rounds go from the weakest to the strongest, because the taste of lemon stays in the mouth. The first round uses 3 drops of plain water, to show how often you swallow anyway. Only one thing changes: what reaches your tongue, your nose or your thoughts.

materials.item: a lemon or lime. A piece of tamarind soaked in a spoon of water also works
a knife, for a grown-up to cut the lemon
teaspoons, one for water and one for lemon juice
a tumbler of drinking water
a clock or a phone timer
a pencil and a notebook page for the results

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the lemon with the knife.
experiments.record: Draw a table with four rows: water drops, thinking, smelling and tasting. Write the number of swallows in 2 minutes for each round.
experiments.context: In this experiment you count how often you swallow in 2 minutes. You compare plain water, thinking about a lemon, smelling a lemon and tasting lemon juice.

setup.art: A child sitting with lips closed and one finger raised, while a grown-up beside her makes a tally mark and watches a phone timer.
setup.caption: 1. Keep your lips closed. Raise a finger each time you swallow. A helper counts for 2 minutes.

setup.art: A grown-up letting three drops of water fall from a teaspoon onto a child's tongue.
setup.caption: 2. Round 1: 3 drops of plain water on the tongue.

setup.art: The child with eyes closed and empty hands, and the grown-up reading from a notebook.
setup.caption: 3. Round 2: eyes closed. Think about biting a lemon. No lemon is in the room yet.

setup.art: The child with eyes closed sniffing half a cut lemon held under her nose.
setup.caption: 4. Round 3: smell a cut lemon. Do not touch it.

setup.art: The grown-up letting three drops of lemon juice fall from a teaspoon onto the child's tongue.
setup.caption: 5. Round 4: 3 drops of lemon juice on the tongue. Write every count.

flow.do: Keep the lemon out of sight. Explain the four rounds. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will count how often you swallow in 2 minutes. You will think about a lemon, smell one and taste one. Which will make your mouth water most? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which will make your mouth water most: thinking, smelling or tasting? Why?

ask.q: Do you think only thinking about a lemon will make your mouth water? Why?
good: Yes, my mouth waters when I think of sour things.
No, nothing is touching my tongue.
A little, but less than the real juice.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most people are sure that a thought alone makes the mouth water a lot. The test checks that belief.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Lemon Test. You guess what will make your mouth water most, before you test.

flow.do: Practise. Your child sits still with lips closed and raises a finger at each swallow. Count for 1 minute. Then draw the results table with four rows.
flow.say: Keep your lips closed. Swallow only when your mouth feels full, and raise a finger each time. I will count. This minute is only for practice.
flow.kid: Keep your lips closed. Raise a finger each time you swallow.
flow.parent: You can also watch the bump at the front of the throat. It rises with each swallow. One or two swallows a minute is usual at rest.
flow.context: In this step of the Lemon Test you practise counting swallows before the four rounds begin.

flow.do: Round 1. Put 3 drops of plain water on the middle of your child's tongue with a teaspoon. Count swallows for 2 minutes. Write the number. Rest for 1 minute.
flow.say: Round 1. Here are 3 drops of plain water. Lips closed. I am counting for 2 minutes.
flow.kid: Round 1. Three drops of water. Lips closed. Raise a finger for each swallow.

check.q: Why does the Lemon Test begin with 3 drops of plain water?
options: To show how often I swallow anyway
To make the lemon taste stronger
check.why: Everyone swallows now and then. The water round gives that number. A later round counts as 'more' only if it is clearly above the water round.

flow.context: In this step of the Lemon Test you count your swallows after 3 drops of plain water.

flow.do: Round 2. Your child closes their eyes. Read the words in the note slowly. Count swallows for 2 minutes from the first word. Write the number. Rest for 1 minute with one sip of water.
flow.say: Round 2. Close your eyes and listen. I will describe a lemon. Keep counting your swallows with your finger.
flow.kid: Round 2. Close your eyes. Think about the lemon. Raise a finger for each swallow.
flow.parent: Read this slowly: 'Picture a bright yellow lemon. I cut it in half. Juice runs out on the plate. You pick up one half. You bite into it. The sour juice fills your mouth.' Then stay quiet until the 2 minutes end.
flow.context: In this step of the Lemon Test you count your swallows while you only think about a lemon.

flow.do: Round 3. Cut the lemon in half. Your child closes their eyes. Hold one half about 3 centimetres under their nose for 2 minutes. Count swallows. Write the number. Rest for 1 minute with one sip of water.
flow.say: Round 3. Eyes closed. I am holding a cut lemon under your nose. Breathe through your nose. Do not touch the lemon.
flow.kid: Round 3. Eyes closed. Smell the lemon. Raise a finger for each swallow.
flow.context: In this step of the Lemon Test you count your swallows while you smell a cut lemon.

flow.do: Round 4. Squeeze a little juice into the second teaspoon. Put 3 drops on the middle of your child's tongue. Count swallows for 2 minutes. Write the number.
flow.say: Round 4. Here are 3 drops of lemon juice. Lips closed. I am counting for 2 minutes.
flow.kid: Round 4. Three drops of lemon juice. Lips closed. Raise a finger for each swallow.
flow.parent: Ask your child to notice how soon the mouth begins to water. It usually starts within a second or two.
flow.context: In this step of the Lemon Test you count your swallows after 3 drops of lemon juice.

flow.do: Look at the four numbers together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your four counts. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Did you decide to make saliva in round 4?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Which rounds were clearly above the water round?
good: The lemon juice round.
Only the taste, the others were about the same.
Smelling was a little more.

ask.q: How do you think the message got from your tongue to the glands that make saliva?
good: By nerves, because it was so fast.
It went to my brain and back.
It was a reflex.

flow.parent: Most people swallow about twice as often after the lemon juice as after the water. Thinking and smelling often add little or nothing. Write down what you really found. The reason: sensors on the tongue detect the acid in the juice. A nerve signal goes to the brain stem, the lowest part of the brain. A signal comes straight back along other nerves to the glands that make saliva. This is a reflex, and it starts within a second or two. The mouth can also learn to water at a smell or a thought. In careful tests that effect is small, and some people show none.
flow.think: Saliva starts in about a second. What does that speed tell you about the messenger?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Lemon Test. You compare your four counts and say what they show about a reflex.

activities.title: Did I Decide That? Two things your body does before you choose

materials.item: a pencil with a blunt end
a notebook page

schedule.what: Try a clap near the face, a stroke on the sole of the foot and a spoken request. Do each one 5 times.

activities.record: A table with three rows: clap, sole of the foot, and 'touch your nose'. For each, write how many times out of 5 the body answered, and whether you chose to do it.
activities.context: In this activity a helper claps near your face and strokes the sole of your foot. The helper also asks you to touch your nose. You find out which answers you chose and which ones your body gave first.

setup.art: A grown-up clapping her hands once about 30 centimetres in front of a child's face, and the child's eyes shut tight.
setup.caption: 1. A helper claps once in front of your face. Do your eyes blink?

setup.art: A child sitting with one bare foot on a grown-up's lap, and the grown-up stroking the sole from heel to toes with the blunt end of a pencil.
setup.caption: 2. The helper strokes the sole of your foot with a blunt pencil. What do your toes do?

setup.art: A child touching the tip of her nose with one finger while a grown-up speaks to her.
setup.caption: 3. The helper says 'touch your nose'. You may do it or not.

flow.do: Draw the table with three rows. Explain the three tests. Ask which actions your child thinks they will choose.
flow.say: I will clap near your face, stroke your foot and ask you to touch your nose. Which of your answers will you choose? Which will just happen?
flow.kid: Draw three rows: clap, foot, nose. Which answers will you choose?
flow.context: This is the first step of Did I Decide That. You draw the table and guess which answers you will choose.

flow.do: Sit facing your child. At a surprise moment, clap your hands once, about 30 centimetres in front of their face. Watch their eyes. Do this 5 times, with gaps of different lengths. Count the blinks.
flow.say: Look at my nose and keep your eyes open. I will clap when you do not expect it. Did you choose to blink just then?
flow.kid: Keep your eyes open. A helper claps near your face. Did you blink?
flow.parent: Clap in front of the face, never beside an ear. Most children blink at the first claps. The blink may fade by the fifth clap, because the body learns that the clap is harmless.
flow.context: In this step of Did I Decide That a helper claps near your face 5 times and counts your blinks.

flow.do: Your child sits with one bare foot on your lap and looks away. Stroke the sole firmly from heel to toes with the blunt end of the pencil. Do this 5 times. Watch the toes and the leg.
flow.say: Look at the wall and not at your foot. I will stroke the sole of your foot. Tell me what your toes and your leg did.
flow.kid: Look away. A helper strokes the sole of your foot. What do your toes do?
flow.parent: The toes usually curl and the foot pulls back. A firm stroke works better than a light one, which only tickles.
flow.context: In this step of Did I Decide That a helper strokes the sole of your foot. You watch what your toes do.

flow.do: Say 'touch your nose' 5 times, with gaps. Your child may do it or not, as they like. Fill in the table. Then talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Now I will say 'touch your nose' 5 times. Do it or not, as you choose. How was this different from the clap and the foot?
flow.kid: A helper says 'touch your nose'. Do it or not. How is this different?

ask.q: What was the same about the blink and the foot pulling back?
good: I did not choose them.
They were very fast.
They happened the same way each time.
They protect my eye and my foot.

check.q: What do we call a quick answer that the body gives without waiting for a decision?
check.why: A reflex is fast and needs no decision, like a blink at a clap. A hormone is a chemical in the blood. A habit is something you learned by doing it often.

flow.context: This is the last step of Did I Decide That. You compare a chosen action with the blink and the foot reflex.

activities.title: Squeeze Chain: time a nerve message through two bodies

materials.item: a phone stopwatch, or a clock with a seconds hand
a notebook page and a pencil
two people. More people make a longer chain

schedule.what: Pass 20 hand squeezes back and forth with your eyes closed, and time them three times.

activities.record: Write the time for 20 squeezes on each of three tries. Circle the middle time. Divide it by 20 to find the time for one pass.
activities.context: In this activity two people hold hands with eyes closed. A squeeze goes back and forth 20 times, and you time it to find how long one pass takes.

setup.art: A grown-up and a child sitting on the floor facing each other with eyes closed, holding one hand each, while the grown-up's free hand rests on a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 1. Sit facing each other. Hold one hand. The helper's other hand is on the stopwatch.

setup.art: A close view of two joined hands, one squeezing the other.
setup.caption: 2. When you feel a squeeze, squeeze back at once. Do not guess the beat.

setup.art: A notebook page showing three times in seconds, with the middle one circled and a division sum beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Time 20 squeezes, three times. Divide the middle time by 20.

flow.do: Explain the chain. Ask your child to guess how many seconds 20 squeezes will take, and why. Write the guess down.
flow.say: I will squeeze your hand. When you feel it, squeeze back. Then I squeeze again. How many seconds will 20 squeezes take? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A squeeze goes back and forth 20 times. How many seconds will it take?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Squeeze Chain. You guess how long 20 hand squeezes will take.

flow.do: Sit facing each other and hold one hand. Both close your eyes. Practise 10 squeezes back and forth. Each squeeze is short and firm.
flow.say: Eyes closed. Squeeze only when you feel my squeeze, and never before it. Short and firm. Let us practise ten.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Squeeze back only when you feel a squeeze.
flow.parent: With three or more people, sit in a line and hold hands. The squeeze travels down the line and back again.
flow.context: In this step of the Squeeze Chain you practise passing a squeeze with your eyes closed.

flow.do: Start the stopwatch with your free hand as you give the first squeeze. Count your own squeezes silently. Stop the watch when you feel your child's tenth squeeze. That makes 20 squeezes. Do this three times and write each time.
flow.say: Now we time it. Twenty squeezes, ten from each of us. Eyes closed. I start now.
flow.kid: Eyes closed. Twenty squeezes, ten from each of you. A helper times it.
flow.parent: Most pairs take 4 to 6 seconds. A time under 3 seconds means you both fell into a beat and squeezed before you felt the squeeze. Try again more slowly.
flow.context: In this step of the Squeeze Chain you time 20 squeezes, three times.

flow.do: Circle the middle time of the three. Divide it by 20 to find the time for one pass. Talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Take the middle time and divide it by 20. That is the time for one pass. Where did the message travel inside you during that time?
flow.kid: Divide the middle time by 20. Where did the message go inside you?

ask.q: Where did the message travel between the squeeze you felt and the squeeze you gave?
good: From my hand up my arm to my spinal cord.
Up to my brain.
Back down the same arm to my hand muscles.

flow.parent: One pass usually takes about a quarter of a second. The message travels about 2 metres along nerves, which takes only a few hundredths of a second. Most of the time is spent in the brain and in getting the muscles to move.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Squeeze Chain. You work out the time for one pass and trace the path of the message.

activities.title: Wool Paths: measure a reflex path on your own body

materials.item: wool or string, about 4 metres
scissors
a ruler or a measuring tape
a notebook page and a pencil

schedule.what: Lay one piece of wool along the reflex path and one along the path through the brain, then measure both.

activities.record: Write the length of the reflex path and the length of the brain path in centimetres. Write the difference between them.
activities.context: In this activity you lay wool along your arm and back to show two paths a message can take. One turns round in the spinal cord, and the other goes up to the brain first.

setup.art: A child standing with one arm held out sideways while a grown-up lays a piece of red wool from her fingertip along the arm to the middle of her upper back.
setup.caption: 1. Lay wool from a fingertip, along the arm, to the backbone between the shoulders.

setup.art: The wool continuing from the backbone back along the shoulder to the front of the upper arm, where the grown-up holds it against the muscle.
setup.caption: 2. Bring the wool back to the front of the upper arm. Cut it. This is the reflex path.

setup.art: A second piece of blue wool going from the fingertip to the backbone, up the neck to the top of the head, back down, and out to the upper arm.
setup.caption: 3. The second wool goes up to the top of the head and down again. This is the brain path.

setup.art: Two pieces of wool lying straight on the floor beside a measuring tape, one clearly longer than the other.
setup.caption: 4. Measure both pieces of wool. Find the difference.

flow.do: Explain the two paths. Ask your child to guess how much longer the path through the brain is, and whether that extra length matters.
flow.say: A fingertip touches a hot pot. One message turns round in the spinal cord. Another goes up to the brain first. How much longer is the second path? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One path turns in the spinal cord. One goes to the brain. How much longer?
flow.context: This is the first step of Wool Paths. You guess how much longer the path through the brain is.

flow.do: Your child holds one arm out sideways. Hold the wool at the tip of the middle finger. Lay it along the arm to the backbone between the shoulder blades. Bring it back along the shoulder to the front of the upper arm. Cut it there.
flow.say: This wool is the reflex path. The message goes in from the fingertip to the spinal cord. It comes out to the muscle that bends your elbow.
flow.kid: Hold your arm out. A helper lays wool from fingertip to backbone to arm muscle.
flow.parent: The real nerve fibres run inside the arm and inside the backbone. The wool on the skin follows nearly the same route.
flow.context: In this step of Wool Paths you lay wool along the reflex path. It runs from fingertip to spinal cord to arm muscle.

flow.do: Take a new piece of wool. Lay it from the fingertip to the backbone as before. Then take it up the back of the neck to the top of the head. Bring it back down to the same place. Bring it out to the front of the upper arm. Cut it.
flow.say: This wool is the brain path. The message goes up to the top of the brain, where touch is felt. Then an order comes all the way back down.
flow.kid: The second wool goes up to the top of your head. Then it comes back down.
flow.context: In this step of Wool Paths you lay wool along the path that goes through the brain.

flow.do: Lay both pieces straight on the floor and measure them. Work out the difference. Then talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Measure both paths. A fast nerve signal covers 50 centimetres in one hundredth of a second. How much time does the extra length cost?
flow.kid: Measure both pieces of wool. How much longer is the brain path?

ask.q: The extra length costs only about one hundredth of a second. So why is a reflex so much quicker than a chosen action?
good: The reflex path has fewer synapses.
Nobody has to decide anything.
The brain takes time to work out what to do.

check.q: What is the main reason that a reflex is quicker than a chosen action?
check.why: The reflex path crosses only one or two synapses in the spinal cord. A chosen action passes through many synapses in the brain while the brain works out what to do. The extra length of the path adds very little time.

flow.parent: For a child of nine the reflex path is about 1 metre and the brain path about 1.5 metres. The difference in length is small. The real saving is in synapses and in deciding.
flow.context: This is the last step of Wool Paths. You measure the reflex path and the brain path and compare them.

activities.title: A Tug and a Drop: model the two kinds of message

materials.item: string or thick thread, about 2 metres
clear glass tumblers or clean glass jars, filled with water
ink or food colour, 2 drops. Strong tea or coffee decoction also works
a spoon
a clock or a phone timer

schedule.what: Send a tug along a string, then watch a drop of colour spread through water with and without a stir.

activities.record: Draw the tumbler without a stir at 10 seconds, 1 minute and 3 minutes. Write how many seconds the stirred tumbler took to become one even colour.
activities.context: In this activity a tug on a string stands for a nerve message. A drop of colour in water stands for a hormone, and a stir with a spoon stands for the heart.

setup.art: Two people standing two metres apart holding the ends of a tight string, one with eyes closed.
setup.caption: 1. Hold a string tight between two people. One tugs. The other feels it at once.

setup.art: A clear glass tumbler of still water with one dark drop of ink sinking and trailing thin streaks.
setup.caption: 2. Put one drop of colour into still water. Do not stir. Watch for 3 minutes.

setup.art: A second tumbler being stirred once with a spoon, the colour swirling evenly through the water.
setup.caption: 3. Put one drop into the second tumbler. Stir once. Count the seconds until the colour is even.

flow.do: Fill both tumblers with water and leave them still on a table. Cut the string. Explain that you will send a message in two ways.
flow.say: We will send a message along a string. Then we will send one through water. Which will arrive first? Which will reach more places?
flow.kid: Fill two tumblers with water. Leave them still. Cut the string.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Tug and a Drop. You set out the string and two tumblers of still water.

flow.do: You and your child hold the ends of the string and pull it tight. Your child closes their eyes. Tug once at a surprise moment. Your child says 'now' when they feel it. Swap over and repeat.
flow.say: Eyes closed. Say 'now' when you feel my tug. Did the tug reach anyone else in the room?
flow.kid: Hold the string tight. Close your eyes. Say 'now' when you feel a tug.

ask.q: How is the tug like a nerve message?
good: It arrives at once.
It only reaches the person at the end of the string.
It stops when the tugging stops.

flow.context: In this step of A Tug and a Drop you send a tug along a tight string. The tug is a model of a nerve message.

flow.do: Put one drop of colour into the first tumbler. Do not touch it. Your child draws it after 10 seconds, 1 minute and 3 minutes.
flow.say: This drop is a hormone leaving a gland. The water is the blood. Watch where the colour goes. Draw it three times.
flow.kid: Put one drop of colour in still water. Do not stir. Draw what you see.
flow.parent: After 3 minutes the colour is still in streaks and patches. Left alone, it would take hours to become even.
flow.context: In this step of A Tug and a Drop you watch a drop of colour spread through still water. The drop is a model of a hormone.

flow.do: Put one drop into the second tumbler and stir once with the spoon. Count the seconds until the colour is even. Then talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Now one drop and one stir. Count the seconds until the colour is even. In your body, what does the job that the spoon did?
flow.kid: One drop, one stir. Count the seconds until the colour is even.

ask.q: In your body, what does the job of the spoon?
good: The heart.
The heart pumps the blood round, so the hormone is mixed in.

check.q: A hormone spreads through the whole body in about one minute. What makes that possible?
options: The heart pumps the blood round
check.why: The heart pumps all your blood round your body in about one minute, and the hormone is carried with it. Without that pumping, a hormone would drift as slowly as the colour in the still tumbler.

flow.parent: The model leaves one thing out. In the body, only cells with the right receptor answer the hormone. In the tumbler, the colour reaches everything alike.
flow.context: This is the last step of A Tug and a Drop. You compare still water with stirred water and say what stands for the heart.

projects.title: My Slow Clocks: three days of hunger and sleepiness

materials.item: a notebook page for the chart
a pencil and two colour pencils
a clock

schedule.what: Draw the chart. Rate your hunger and your sleepiness at six set times.
Rate hunger and sleepiness at the same six times.
Rate at the same six times, draw the lines and look for the pattern.

projects.record: A chart with six times across the top and three days down the side. In each box write two numbers from 0 to 3: one for hunger and one for sleepiness.
projects.context: In this three-day project you rate how hungry and how sleepy you are at six set times each day. You look for a pattern that repeats, which shows slow hormone messages at work.

setup.art: A notebook chart with six clock times across the top and rows for Day 1, Day 2 and Day 3, each box holding two small numbers.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a chart with six times a day, for three days.

setup.art: A child looking at a wall clock before lunch and writing two numbers in the chart.
setup.caption: 2. At each time, rate your hunger and your sleepiness from 0 to 3. Rate before you eat.

setup.art: The finished chart with a red line for hunger and a blue line for sleepiness drawn across each day.
setup.caption: 3. On day 3, draw the lines and look for what repeats.

flow.do: Choose six times that fit your day: on waking, mid-morning, just before lunch, mid-afternoon, just before dinner and at bedtime. Draw the chart. Your child rates hunger and sleepiness at each time today.
flow.say: At six times each day you will rate two things from 0 to 3. One is how hungry you are, and the other is how sleepy you are. Do you think the numbers will repeat from day to day? Why?
flow.kid: Six times a day, rate your hunger from 0 to 3. Rate your sleepiness too.

ask.q: What do you think makes you hungry at lunch time?
good: My stomach is empty.
It is the time I usually eat.
I smell the food.

flow.parent: Rate before eating, not after. Do not correct the guess. Set phone reminders for the six times if that helps.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Slow Clocks. You draw the chart and start rating your hunger and sleepiness.

flow.do: Your child rates hunger and sleepiness at the same six times. If a meal is late today, they still rate at the usual time, before eating.
flow.say: Same six times as before. Rate your hunger and your sleepiness before you look at the earlier numbers.
flow.kid: Rate hunger and sleepiness at the same six times. Do not peek at the old numbers.
flow.wait: Do this the day after you draw the chart
flow.context: In this step of My Slow Clocks you rate your hunger and sleepiness on the second day.

flow.do: After the last rating, your child joins each day's hunger numbers with a red line. They join the sleepiness numbers with a blue line. Look at the three days together. Then read the note below.
flow.say: Draw a red line for hunger and a blue line for sleepiness. At which times is each line highest? Is it the same on all three days?
flow.kid: Draw a red line for hunger and a blue line for sleepiness. What repeats?
flow.wait: Do this on the third day, after the bedtime rating

ask.q: Did hunger rise before your usual meal times, even before you saw any food?
good: Yes, I was hungry just before lunch every day.
Yes, even when lunch was late.
Mine was not so regular.

flow.parent: Most children find that hunger peaks just before their usual meals. Sleepiness rises at about the same time each night. Two hormones are part of the reason. The stomach wall releases a hormone called ghrelin, which the brain reads as hunger. In a study in 2001, ghrelin in people's blood rose shortly before each meal. In the dark of evening a small gland in the brain releases melatonin. It tells the body that night has come. If your child's chart is irregular, that is a real result too. Late nights, snacks and screens all shift these rhythms.
flow.context: This is the last step of My Slow Clocks. You draw lines for three days of hunger and sleepiness and look for a repeating pattern.

challenges.title: Build a Reflex: the short path must finish first
challenges.problem: A hand must leave a hot pot before the brain has finished thinking. Build a model with falling pieces. One push at the 'fingertip' must start two paths. The short path ends at the 'muscle' plate. The long path ends at the 'brain' plate. The last piece must land on the muscle plate first.
constraints: Only one push, on the first piece.
Both paths start from that same first piece.
The brain path has at least twice as many pieces as the muscle path.
After the push, nobody touches anything.
The muscle plate must sound first on 3 tries in a row.
materials: about 25 small things that stand on end and tip over. Dominoes, matchboxes, erasers, building blocks or small empty cartons all work
2 steel plates or lids, one for the end of each path
paper and a pencil for the design
general: Stand the pieces in one line. Where the paths split, place two pieces side by side so that one falling piece hits both.
Make the muscle path short and straight. Let the brain path curve away in a long loop.
Put a steel plate where the last piece of each path will fall, so that you hear it land.
creative: Leave a gap in one path and bridge it with a ruler balanced on an eraser. The gap is a synapse, and the ruler is the chemical that crosses it.
Make a second path that comes back from the brain plate towards the muscle. It is the brain's own order, which arrives later.
Stand a book in the muscle path as a gate. It is the brain stopping the reflex, as when you hold on to a hot cup.
challenges.your_turn: Now model a reflex of your own choice, such as a blink or a sneeze. Draw where its message starts, where it turns round and where it ends. Build it, test it 3 times and write what happened.
challenges.context: In this challenge you build two paths of falling pieces from one starting point. The short path stands for a reflex, and the long path stands for a message to the brain.

setup.art: A line of matchboxes standing on end on a floor, splitting into a short straight row and a long curved row, each ending at a steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. Stand the pieces in two paths from one starting piece. End each path at a steel plate.

setup.art: A child's finger pushing the first matchbox, and the fall moving along both rows.
setup.caption: 2. Push the first piece once. Do not touch anything else.

setup.art: The last piece of the short row lying on its steel plate while the long row is still falling.
setup.caption: 3. Listen. Which plate sounds first? Test 3 times.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Collect the pieces. Ask your child to draw the two paths on paper and label fingertip, spinal cord, muscle and brain.
flow.say: One push starts two paths. Which path stands for the reflex? Which stands for the message to the brain? Draw them before you build.
flow.kid: Draw two paths from one start. Label the muscle end and the brain end.

ask.q: Where on your drawing is the spinal cord?
good: Where the two paths split.
At the place where the message turns back towards the muscle.

flow.parent: Any flat things of the same size that stand on end will do. Test three pieces first to find a spacing that works, usually about half the height of a piece.
flow.context: This is the first step of Build a Reflex. You plan a short path and a long path of falling pieces.

flow.do: Your child builds both paths and puts a steel plate at the end of each. Help only to steady the pieces.
flow.say: Build the muscle path first, then the brain path. Count the pieces in each. Is the brain path at least twice as long?
flow.kid: Build both paths. Put a steel plate at each end. Count the pieces.
flow.context: In this step of Build a Reflex you build the two paths. You put a steel plate at the end of each.

flow.do: Test it. Your child pushes the first piece once. Listen for which plate sounds first. Set the pieces up again and test until it works 3 times in a row.
flow.say: One push, then hands off. Which plate did you hear first? Set the pieces up and try again.
flow.kid: Push the first piece once. Which plate sounds first? Test three times.
flow.context: In this step of Build a Reflex you test the model 3 times and listen for which plate sounds first.

flow.do: Add one idea from the creative list, or your child's own. Test again. Then talk about the question below.
flow.say: Add one new part and test again. Now compare the model with a real nerve. What is the same? What is different?
flow.kid: Add one new part. Test again. How is this like a real nerve?

ask.q: After a signal, a real nerve fibre is ready again in a few thousandths of a second. How is your model different?
good: I have to stand every piece up again by hand.
A nerve resets itself.
The nerve uses energy from food to reset.

flow.parent: The model shows two true things. Each piece stays in place while the fall travels, as ions stay near their spot while the signal travels. A path with fewer pieces finishes sooner, as a path with fewer synapses does.
flow.context: This is the last step of Build a Reflex. You add a part to the model and compare it with a real nerve.

items.p: What carries a nerve message from your fingertip to your spinal cord?
items.why: A nerve message is a signal that travels along nerve fibres. Blood carries hormones, which are the other kind of message.

items.p: What carries a hormone from a gland to the cells it changes?
items.why: A gland puts the hormone into the blood, and the heart pumps the blood round the body. If you chose nerve fibres, you were thinking of the fast kind of message.

items.p: A quick answer that the body gives without waiting for a decision is called a ____.
items.why: A reflex is fast and needs no decision. Blinking at a clap and pulling a hand from a hot pot are reflexes.

items.p: A hormone message usually arrives faster than a nerve message.
items.why: False. A nerve message arrives in a fraction of a second. A hormone must be released and carried by the blood, and its effect takes from seconds to hours.

items.p: Match each hormone to what it tells the body to do.
items.why: Each hormone fits the receptors of its own target cells. So each one gives a different order to a different part of the body.

items.p: Sort these. Is each message carried mainly by nerves or by a hormone?
items: pale pee after a lot of water
sugar leaving the blood after a meal
items.why: Ask how fast it happens and where. A quick answer in one place is the work of nerves. A slow change across the body is the work of a hormone.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to show what happens when a fingertip touches a hot pot.
items: The fingertip touches the hot pot
A signal travels up the arm nerve
The signal crosses a synapse in the spinal cord
A signal travels down to the arm muscle
a: The fingertip touches the hot pot
A signal travels up the arm nerve
The signal crosses a synapse in the spinal cord
A signal travels down to the arm muscle
items.why: The message turns round in the spinal cord, so the hand moves first. The news reaches the brain by a longer path, so the pain is felt last.

items.p: In the Water Message Test, both days started at the same time of day. Why?
opts: So only the drink was different
So the clock was easier to read
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing. The body handles water differently in the morning and at night. Keeping the time the same leaves the drink as the only difference.

items.p: The tiny gap between one neuron and the next cell is called a ____.
items.why: At a synapse a chemical carries the message across the gap. Each synapse adds a small delay.

items.p: Your brain feels the pain before your hand leaves a hot pot.
items.why: False. The hand is pulled away by a reflex through the spinal cord. The message to the brain takes a longer path, so the pain is felt a moment later.

items.p: Where does the message turn round when a hand pulls back from something hot?
items.why: The signal goes in to the spinal cord and crosses one or two synapses. Then it comes straight back out to the arm muscle.

items.p: Explain in two sentences why growing taller is a job for a hormone and not for a nerve.
items.a: Growing is slow and goes on for years in bones all over the body. A hormone in the blood reaches all those bones and can keep working for a long time.
items.why: A strong answer says that the job is slow, long and spread across the body. It also says that blood reaches every part.

items.p: In the Water Message Test, your tongue felt the water at once. Why did your kidneys answer much later?
items.a: The tongue's message went by nerves, which are fast. The water had to pass into the blood first. Then the hormone ADH had to fall before the kidneys let the water out.
items.why: A strong answer says that a hormone in the blood tells the kidneys, and no nerve does. It also says that each step takes minutes.

items.p: Draw an arm and a backbone. Draw a reflex path from a fingertip. Label the spinal cord and the muscle.
items.a: One arrow from the fingertip along the arm to the spinal cord inside the backbone. A second arrow from the spinal cord back out to the muscle of the upper arm.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the message going in and coming out again at the spinal cord. It does not go up to the brain first.
items.art: A blank box with a faint outline of a child's arm, shoulder and backbone.

items.p: Why does adrenaline change the heart but not a fingernail?
opts: The nail has no receptors for it
The nail is too far away
items.why: A hormone changes only cells that have its receptor. Heart muscle cells have receptors for adrenaline. The tip of a nail is not made of living cells, so it has none.

items.p: Which message ends soonest after its sender stops sending?
opts: A nerve signal to a muscle
items.why: A nerve message ends when the signals stop. A hormone stays in the blood until the body has cleared it, which takes minutes or hours.

items.p: What do sodium ions do when a nerve signal passes?
opts: They carry sugar to the brain
items.why: Tiny gates open and sodium ions rush in at one spot. That makes the next gates open, so the change moves along the fibre.

items.p: A person has plenty of a hormone, but their cells lack its receptor. What happens?
opts: The cells do not answer it
The cells answer twice as hard
It turns into a nerve signal
items.why: A hormone works only by fitting its receptor. Without the receptor, the hormone passes the cells and nothing changes, however much there is.

items.p: A fright is over, but the heart still pounds for some minutes. Why?
opts: Adrenaline is still in the blood
The nerves are still sending the fright
items.why: The nerve part of the fright ended at once. The adrenaline goes on working until the body has broken it down.

items.p: Every nerve message is partly chemical.
items.why: True. Along the fibre the signal is electrical. At each synapse a chemical carries the message across the gap.

items.p: A reflex can only happen if the brain decides to start it.
items.why: False. A reflex such as pulling back from heat runs through the spinal cord. It starts before the brain has heard the news.

items.p: Sort these by how soon the body answers.
items: turning the head to a sound
items.why: The answers within seconds are carried by nerves. The slow ones are carried by hormones in the blood.

items.p: Three of these are reflexes. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Blinking, sneezing and mouth-watering happen without a decision. Choosing a book is a decision, and it takes much longer.

items.p: In the Squeeze Chain, 20 squeezes took 5 seconds. How many squeezes passed in one second?
items.why: 20 divided by 5 is 4. So each pass took a quarter of a second.

items.p: Put these in order, to show what happens after you drink 2 tumblers of water.
items: Water passes from the gut into the blood
Sensors in the brain notice that the blood is more watery
The gland under the brain releases less ADH
The kidneys let more water out
Nerves tell the brain that the bladder is full
a: Water passes from the gut into the blood
Sensors in the brain notice that the blood is more watery
The gland under the brain releases less ADH
The kidneys let more water out
Nerves tell the brain that the bladder is full
items.why: The kidneys are told by a hormone, so the middle steps are slow. The last step is a nerve message, so it is fast.

items.p: A dog barks suddenly behind you. Describe what nerves do first and what a hormone does next.
items.a: Nerves carry the sound to my brain and make me jump within a fraction of a second. Nerves also tell the adrenal glands to release adrenaline. The adrenaline keeps my heart pounding for some minutes.
items.why: A strong answer gives the nerve part first and fast, and the hormone part second and lasting.

items.p: The Lemon Test began with drops of plain water. What would be wrong with leaving that round out?
items.a: I would not know how often I swallow anyway. Then I could not tell whether the lemon juice really made more saliva.
items.why: A strong answer says that a result means something only when it is compared with what happens without the lemon.

items.p: Some people say the brain controls everything. Name two things your body does without waiting for the brain.
items.a: My hand pulls back from a hot thing by a reflex in the spinal cord. My pancreas releases insulin when it senses sugar in the blood. My gut moves food along by its own nerves.
items.why: A strong answer gives two true examples. A spinal reflex, a gland that senses the blood and the gut moving food all count.

items.p: Many findings about nerves and hormones came from tests on dogs, frogs and other animals. People disagree about such tests.

views.who: A doctor who treats children with diabetes
views.says: Insulin was found through tests on dogs. It keeps my patients alive every day. Without those tests, they would have died.

views.who: A woman who cares for street dogs
views.says: A dog feels pain and fear through nerves and hormones like ours. That is the very reason we should not use dogs in this way.
We now test many things on cells in a dish first. For some questions there is still no other way. The law says the animals must be given pain relief.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason that uses what you know about nerves and hormones. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that other animals have the same nerves, reflexes and hormones as we do. That is why the tests teach us about our bodies, and also why the animals can suffer.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer sees that the same fact, that our bodies work alike, supports more than one side.

items.p: Label four parts on this drawing of a reflex arc: sensor in the skin, spinal cord, synapse and muscle.
a: Sensor in the skin: at the fingertip, where the signal starts
Spinal cord: inside the backbone, where the message turns round
Synapse: the gap inside the spinal cord where one neuron passes the message to the next
Muscle: in the upper arm, where the message ends and the arm bends
items.why: A reflex arc has a start, a turning point and an end. The synapse is at the turning point, inside the spinal cord.
items.art: A drawing of an arm and backbone with a line from the fingertip to the backbone and back to the upper arm, a small gap marked inside the backbone, and four blank label lines.

items.p: Scientists cut every nerve to a piece of gut. The pancreas still answered it. What did this show?
opts: The message travelled in the blood
items.why: With no nerve left, only the blood still joined the two parts. So the message had to be a chemical in the blood. This is how hormones were found.

items.p: A touch on a giraffe's foot takes longer to be felt than a touch on a mouse's foot. Why?
opts: The signal has further to travel
Giraffes have no nerves in the legs
items.why: A nerve signal takes time to travel. A giraffe's signal has several metres to cover, and a mouse's only a few centimetres.

items.p: Which change would make a nerve message take longer to arrive?
items.why: Each synapse adds a small delay, because a chemical must cross the gap. A shorter fibre would make the message arrive sooner.

items.p: Some asthma medicines fit the adrenaline receptors of the airways. What do they do there?
items.why: Adrenaline tells the muscle round the airways to relax, so the airways widen. A medicine that fits the same receptor gives the same order.

items.p: Plants send signals from leaf to leaf, although they have no neurons.
items.why: True. Plants carry electrical signals and use hormones. A touch-me-not folds as an electrical signal passes along the leaf.

items.p: A signal in a nerve travels about as fast as electricity in a copper wire.
items.why: False. The fastest nerve signals travel at about 100 metres per second. Electricity in a wire is millions of times faster.

items.p: Match each part to its job in sending messages.
pairs: Passes a message across a gap
Releases a hormone into the blood
items.why: Sensors and synapses belong to the nerve system. Glands and receptors belong to the hormone system. Synapses also use receptors, which is one way the two systems are alike.

items.p: A fast nerve signal covers 1 metre in 2 hundredths of a second. How many hundredths for a 4-metre path?
items.why: 4 times 2 is 8. So a signal along a giraffe's 4-metre path takes 8 hundredths of a second.

items.p: A cell that has the receptor for a hormone is called a ____ cell.
items.why: Only target cells answer a hormone. All the other cells are passed by.

items.p: On a very hot day, the Water Message Test took 100 minutes. Use ADH to explain why.
items.a: On a hot day the body loses water as sweat. More ADH is in the blood, so the kidneys save water. The extra drink is kept, not sent out.
items.why: A strong answer links the long wait to the body being short of water. It names ADH as the message that tells the kidneys to save water.

items.p: How could you test whether the smell of frying onions makes your mouth water? Say what you would count.
items.a: I would count my swallows for 2 minutes with no smell. Then I would count for 2 minutes while I smell frying onions. I would keep everything else the same and do it more than once.
items.why: A strong answer has something to count, a round without the smell to compare with, and one thing changed.

items.p: The body clears adrenaline from the blood within minutes. Why would it be a problem if adrenaline stayed for days?
items.a: The heart would go on beating hard and the liver would go on letting out sugar. This would continue long after the danger had passed. The body would be worn out, and it could not rest or sleep well.
items.why: A strong answer sees that a message must also end. A hormone that is never cleared goes on giving an order that is no longer needed.

items.p: A reflex moves your hand before you feel pain. Give one benefit of this and one risk.
items.a: It helps because my hand leaves the hot thing sooner, so the burn is smaller. It could go wrong if I were carrying a pot of hot dal, because my hand might let go.
items.why: A strong answer shows that the reflex is fast because it does not check with the brain first. That has a cost as well as a gain.

items.p: A touch-me-not folds their leaves when touched. Scientists agree on what happens, but they disagree about the words to use.

views.says: Plants send electrical signals and use chemicals that neurons also use. The name 'plant neurobiology' helps people notice how much plants do.
Plants have no neurons and no synapses. Borrowed words make people picture a brain that is not there. Plants deserve their own words.
I do not mind which word is used. My touch-me-not folds when I touch them and opens again later. I want to know how they do it.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason that uses what you know about nerve signals and hormones. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that a plant's signal is electrical and travels along the leaf, as a nerve signal does. Another is that a plant has no fibres that end at synapses, so the path is different.
items.why: This is a real disagreement about names. A strong answer says what is the same in plants and animals and what is different. It also says why the choice of word matters.

items.p: Draw one hormone in the blood passing three different cells. Show which cell answers, and show why.
items.a: A blood vessel with small dots in it, passing three cells. One cell has a receptor shaped to fit the dots, and a dot sits in it. The other two cells have no such receptor.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the hormone reaching all three cells, and the receptor as the only difference between them.

quiz.p: Which sentence about a nerve message is true?
opts: It travels along fibres to one place
quiz.why: A nerve message travels along nerve fibres and arrives where those fibres end. The other three answers describe a hormone message.

opts: A chemical message carried by the blood
quiz.why: A gland releases a hormone into the blood, and the blood carries it round the body. If you chose a nerve fibre, you were thinking of the fast kind of message.

opts: Pee turning pale after a drink
quiz.why: A reflex is carried by nerves and is over in a fraction of a second. The other three are the work of hormones and take minutes, hours or months.

quiz.p: You step on a sharp stone and your foot lifts at once. Where did the message turn round?
quiz.why: The signal went up a nerve to the spinal cord and straight back down to the leg muscles. The brain heard about it a moment later.

quiz.p: What must a cell have in order to answer a hormone?
opts: A receptor that the hormone fits
A nerve fibre of its own
quiz.why: A hormone fits its receptor as a key fits a lock. Being near the gland does not matter, because the blood carries the hormone everywhere.

quiz.p: You run the Water Message Test on two days. What must be the same on both days?
opts: Time of day and an empty bladder
quiz.why: The amount of water is the one thing that changes. Everything else that could change the result must stay the same. That includes the time of day and how full the bladder is.

quiz.p: A sudden bang makes you jump, and then your heart pounds for minutes. Which messengers were at work?
quiz.why: The jump is fast, so nerves carried it. The pounding goes on after the bang is over, because adrenaline is still in the blood.

quiz.p: How did scientists first show that some messages travel in the blood?
opts: A message arrived with the nerves cut
They asked patients how they felt
They cooled the nerves with ice
quiz.why: In 1902 Bayliss and Starling cut every nerve to a piece of gut. Acid in that piece still made the pancreas pour out juice, so the message had gone by the blood.

quiz.p: What crosses the gap at a synapse?
quiz.why: The end of the nerve fibre lets out a chemical. It drifts across the gap and starts a new signal on the other side.

quiz.p: Why can a hormone message last longer than a nerve message?
opts: The hormone stays in the blood longer
Nerves get tired after one signal
Blood moves more slowly at night
quiz.why: A nerve message ends when the signals stop. A hormone goes on working until the liver and kidneys have cleared it from the blood.

quiz.p: Your hand leaves a hot pot before you feel pain. Why does the pain come later?
opts: The path to the brain has more synapses
quiz.why: The reflex turns round in the spinal cord after one or two synapses. The message to the brain passes more synapses, so it arrives a moment later.

quiz.p: After a meal the pancreas releases insulin. How does the insulin reach a muscle cell in the leg?
opts: It is made in the leg
quiz.why: The pancreas puts insulin into the blood. The heart pumps that blood to every part of the body, including the leg muscles.

applications: A dentist's injection blocks the gates in a nerve fibre for an hour or two. No signal can pass, so the tooth's message never reaches the brain.
People with one kind of diabetes make no insulin. They inject insulin, a hormone given as a medicine, so that their cells can take in sugar.
A person with a severe allergy may carry an adrenaline injection. Adrenaline widens the airways and keeps the blood pressure up until help comes.
A doctor taps below the kneecap with a small rubber hammer. A normal kick shows that the reflex path through the spinal cord is working.
Salt sold for eating in India has iodine added. The thyroid gland in the neck needs iodine to make its hormone.
A robot on Mars is given 'reflexes'. A radio message from Earth takes from about 3 to 22 minutes to arrive. So the robot must avoid rocks without waiting for orders.
Fruit sellers ripen bananas with a gas that is a plant hormone. Gardeners dip cuttings in a powder of another plant hormone to make roots grow.

open_questions.q: How do billions of nerve signals add up to one thought or one feeling?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can record signals from single neurons and from whole brains. Nobody can yet explain how the signals become what a being feels.

open_questions.q: How many hormones does a body make?
open_questions.why_open: New hormones are still being found. A hormone from fat cells was found in 1994, and one from the stomach in 1999. Fat, bone and muscle are now known to act as glands.

open_questions.q: Do the microbes in the gut send messages that change how we feel?
open_questions.why_open: Gut microbes make chemicals that reach the blood and the gut's nerves. In mice these change behaviour. In people the evidence is still thin.

open_questions.q: How does a plant carry a fast signal from leaf to leaf without nerves?
open_questions.why_open: The signals were filmed in 2018, and they use a chemical that neurons also use. Scientists are still working out which cells carry them and how.

open_questions.q: Can a spinal cord that has been cut be helped to carry messages again?
open_questions.why_open: Nerve fibres in the spinal cord hardly grow back by themselves. Since 2018 a few people with injuries have walked again with the help of electrical signals from a small device. It does not yet work for everyone.
