maths.problem: In the Squeeze Chain, 20 squeezes took 5 seconds. What fraction of a second did one pass take?
maths.explain: 5 seconds shared among 20 passes is 5 divided by 20. In 1 second there were 4 passes, so each pass took one quarter of a second.
maths.context: In the Squeeze Chain two people pass a hand squeeze back and forth 20 times with their eyes closed. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: One pass is too quick to time. Timing many passes and sharing the time out gives the time for one.

maths.problem: A nerve pass in the Squeeze Chain took a quarter of a second. The Water Message Test took 40 minutes. How many times longer was the water message?
maths.explain: 40 minutes is 40 times 60, which is 2,400 seconds. Each second holds 4 quarter-seconds. 2,400 times 4 is 9,600.
maths.context: In the Water Message Test you time how long your kidneys take to send out 2 tumblers of water. In the Squeeze Chain you time a hand squeeze passing between two people. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Putting both times into the same unit shows how different the two kinds of message really are.

maths.problem: In Wool Paths, a reflex path was 100 centimetres and the brain path was 150 centimetres. A fast nerve signal covers 50 centimetres in one hundredth of a second. How much time does the extra length cost? Is that enough to explain why a reflex is quicker?
maths.answer: One hundredth of a second. No, that is too little to explain it.
maths.explain: 150 minus 100 is 50 centimetres. The signal covers that in one hundredth of a second. A chosen action is slower by much more than that. So the main saving is in synapses and deciding, not in distance.
maths.context: In Wool Paths you lay wool along your arm and back to measure two paths. One turns round in the spinal cord and the other goes up to the brain. These are made-up lengths.
maths.why_maths: Working out the time for the extra length tests a guess. The guess is that a reflex is quick because its path is short.

maths.problem: Here are swallows counted in 2 minutes in the Lemon Test. Water: 2. Thinking: 2. Smelling: 3. Lemon juice: 6. Which rounds are clearly above the water round? Could the one extra swallow for smelling be chance?
maths.answer: Only the lemon juice round is clearly above. Yes, one extra swallow could easily be chance.
maths.explain: 6 is three times 2, which is a big difference. 3 is only one more than 2. A count of swallows goes up and down by one from try to try anyway. To be sure about smelling, the round would have to be repeated several times.
maths.context: In the Lemon Test you count how often you swallow in 2 minutes. You do this after water, a thought, a smell and lemon juice. These are made-up counts.
maths.why_maths: Comparing each count with the water count, and asking how big a difference is, shows which results mean something.

maths.problem: A fast nerve signal travels 50 metres in one second. In Wool Paths, a child's path from fingertip to brain is about 1 metre. A blue whale's path from tail to brain is about 25 metres. How long does each signal take?
maths.answer: The child's signal takes one fiftieth of a second. The whale's signal takes half a second.
maths.explain: 50 metres take 1 second, so 1 metre takes one fiftieth of a second. 25 metres is half of 50 metres, so the whale's signal takes half of a second.
maths.context: In Wool Paths you measure the path of a nerve message along your own arm and back. A blue whale is the longest animal alive, so a whale's nerves are the longest.
maths.why_maths: Sharing out one second by distance shows why a very long body gets its news later.

maths.problem: Suppose a gland stops releasing ADH when you drink. The ADH left in the blood halves about every 15 minutes. It starts at 16 units. How much is left after 15, 30 and 45 minutes? When is only a quarter left?
maths.answer: 8 units, then 4 units, then 2 units. A quarter is left after 30 minutes.
maths.explain: Half of 16 is 8. Half of 8 is 4. Half of 4 is 2. A quarter of 16 is 4, and that is reached after two halvings, which is 30 minutes.
maths.context: In the Water Message Test your kidneys send out extra water only after the hormone ADH has fallen. The units here are made up to show the pattern.
maths.why_maths: A halving pattern shows why a hormone message fades slowly and never stops all at once.

how_we_found_out.story: Around 1900 the Russian scientist Ivan Pavlov was the world's leading expert on digestion. He had shown that nerves make the mouth water and make the stomach pour out juice. When food leaves the stomach, the pancreas pours out juice too. Pavlov was sure that nerves carried this message as well. In London, on 16 January 1902, William Bayliss and Ernest Starling tested the idea. They worked on a dog who had been put into a deep sleep with a drug. They cut every nerve to one loop of the dog's gut and left only the blood vessels. Then they put weak acid into the loop, as the stomach does. The pancreas still poured out juice. No nerve was left, so the message had to be travelling in the blood. Next they scraped some lining from the gut, mixed it with acid and injected the liquid into a vein. The pancreas answered again. They named the chemical secretin. In 1905 Starling named all such chemical messengers hormones, from a Greek word that means 'to set in motion'.
how_we_found_out.who: William Bayliss and Ernest Starling at University College London. The idea they tested came from Ivan Pavlov's laboratory in St Petersburg.
how_we_found_out.when: The test was done on 16 January 1902. Starling first used the word hormone in lectures in 1905.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That every message in the body travels along nerves. Bayliss and Starling cut all the nerves to a loop of gut. Its message still reached the pancreas, so it had travelled in the blood.
how_we_found_out.art: A laboratory of 1902 with two men in waistcoats at a bench, glass tubes and a brass clock, and a drawing on the wall of a loop of gut joined to the body only by blood vessels.

roots.context: In this unit you timed a slow message with two tumblers of water. You watched a fast one start with drops of lemon juice. Here we ask what these messages say about who is in charge of a body.

deep_truth.truth: In the Lemon Test, your mouth watered within seconds of the juice touching your tongue. In the Water Message Test, your kidneys answered the drink many minutes later. So the parts of your body get news at different times. There is no single moment when all of you knows something.
deep_truth.habit: We picture ourselves as one knower in the head. This knower learns each thing at one moment and then tells the body. But the saliva glands, the spinal cord and the kidneys each receive messages and answer on their own time.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Lemon Test, saliva came within a second or two, before any decision. In the Water Message Test, the kidneys usually answered 30 to 60 minutes after the drink. A hand leaves a hot pot before the brain feels the pain. In 1902, a loop of gut with every nerve cut still sent its message to the pancreas.

three.who_am_i: You are many parts that keep each other informed. Some parts of you answer before the thinking part has heard the news.
three.what_is_life: Every living being sends messages inside their own body. Plants and bacteria send theirs with chemicals and electrical signals, without any neurons.
three.what_is_this_world: The sodium that carries your nerve signals is the same sodium as in sea salt. Your messages are made from the ordinary matter of the Earth.

roots.thread: You began as one cell. That cell divided again and again, and the cells became different from each other: skin, nerve, kidney and bone. Messages are what keep those trillions of cells working as one body. Many traditions teach that everything comes from one source and stays joined to it. In a body you can see one way this is true. The many parts stay one body because they never stop sending each other news.

teachings.teaching: Speech, sight, hearing and the mind quarrel over who is the greatest. Each leaves the body for a year, and the body lives on without them. When the breath begins to leave, all the others are pulled up with it. They beg the breath to stay.
teachings.link: The story is about the breath, and it knows nothing of nerves or hormones. Yet it pictures a body as many powers that depend on each other, with none of them ruling alone. This unit found the same thing in the way the parts send and answer messages.

teachings.teaching: Zhuangzi lists the hundred joints, the nine openings and the six organs of his body. He asks which of them he should feel closest to. He asks whether they are all servants, or whether they take turns as ruler. He leaves the question open.
teachings.link: This is the question that a reflex raises. Your spinal cord moved your hand, your kidneys answered the water, and your brain was told afterwards. Zhuangzi's question about which part rules is still a fair one.

science.text: The gut has its own net of several hundred million neurons. It moves food along by its own reflexes, even when its nerves to the brain are cut. Bayliss and Starling showed this in 1899.

In 1983 Benjamin Libet recorded brain activity before people moved a finger. It began a fraction of a second before they said they had decided. Scientists still argue about what this means for how we decide.

other_view.view: On this view, knowing happens only in the brain. A spinal cord that moves a hand and a kidney that lets water out are responding, and they know nothing. So there is one moment when you know about the hot pot. It is the moment when the signals reach your brain and you feel the pain.

practice.title: Messages already arriving
practice.say: Sit still together and close your eyes. For a minute, notice the messages that are reaching you from inside. Is your stomach full or empty? Is your bladder full? Can you feel your heartbeat? Are you sleepy or awake? Now open your eyes. Which of those messages did you ask for?
practice.kid: Sit still. Close your eyes. Notice your stomach, your heartbeat and how sleepy you are. Which messages did you ask for?

ask: In the Lemon Test your mouth watered before you chose anything. Was that you doing it?
In the Water Message Test your kidneys answered long after you drank. During that wait, did all of you know about the water?
If each part of your body gets the news at a different time, when do you know something?

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step. It has not yet been done at home. The Water Message Test is in the core path. It needs only drinking water, a tumbler and a clock. It takes two days. Each day has about 12 to 15 minutes of doing and up to 90 minutes of quiet waiting. Start it at the beginning of a session, and use the waits for the cards, the story or the game. After 4 sips there is usually little or no need for the toilet within 90 minutes. After 2 tumblers a clear need usually comes in 30 to 60 minutes, with more and paler pee. On a hot day, after hard play or after salty food, the body keeps the water. Then the wait is longer. The steps say to write down what really happens, and a longer wait is itself the hormone at work. The Lemon Test is also in the core path. It needs a lemon or lime, two teaspoons, a timer and a grown-up to cut the lemon. Swallow counts are small numbers. They are usually 1 to 3 in two minutes after water, and about twice that after lemon juice. Thinking and smelling often add nothing, and the unit says so. The rounds run from weakest to strongest because the lemon taste lingers, so the order is not mixed. Did I Decide That needs a helper. The blink at a clap can fade after a few claps, which the step explains. The Squeeze Chain works with two people. Pairs can fall into a beat and squeeze too early. The step gives a warning sign for this: a time under 3 seconds for 20 squeezes. Wool Paths needs about 4 metres of wool or string and a helper. A Tug and a Drop needs two clear glasses. In still water the colour stays in streaks for much longer than 3 minutes, which is the point. Build a Reflex needs about 25 small things that stand on end. Matchboxes and small cartons work on a smooth floor. No part needs a garden, a pet or a wild animal. Some facts need care. Adrenaline in blood is compared with one drop in a large swimming pool, and that is a rough comparison. The time for a reflex is given as 'a fraction of a second' because it varies with the reflex. The halving time of ADH, about 15 minutes, is a rounded figure. The date 16 January 1902 and the word hormone in 1905 are from the standard histories. The Zhuangzi passage is given as a paraphrase.
